en: As soon as she reached him, Khan Saykal
Struck the champion Koyonaaly
In the side as she passed.
Her lacquered spear of tempered iron
Burst apart in eighty places
And flew away shattered.
Your champion Koyonaaly,
Your valiant one, did not budge.
Swift Algara beneath her
Carried her onward in a rush.
Once Saykal had come in front of him,
Once he knew she was an enemy,
Your dear Koyonaaly
Gave a mighty shout.
Before Saykal could turn and recover,
Before she could get into position,
He clutched her once by the broad shoulder blade,
Scooping her up like a fur cap,
And seized Saykal.
When they reached a downward slope,
He swept Saykal from her saddle;
Carrying her like a feedbag,
He vanquished Saykal.
Your champion Koyonaaly,
Showing he was a hero,
Swept Saykal up
And set her upon his saddle bow.
She was caught in a crushing hold;
When he squeezed her once,
Her rib bones crackled.
Saykal, Karacha’s daughter,
Then burst into shrieking tears.
When the boy pressed her hard,
Her many sorrows overflowed her heart;
Her tears streamed in ten channels.
Her back bent double;
With her life scarcely hanging on,
Her eyes bulged out.
Her feet dangled,
Her eyes rolled wildly;
In panic she struggled desperately,
And then she began
To plead with your dear Koyonaaly:
“You look like a taker of souls by night—
Grim-looking one, where have you come from?
You resemble my brother-in-law Kökbörü,
Your face resembles my elder sister Külnaary’s.
I shall heed what you say;
My child, I shall go wherever you drive me!
Do not spill my blood here,
Do not take my life in the end!
Here are my mighty people, with their ruler;
If you would cut off my head, here I am!”
“If you do not know my great name,
Unfortunate woman, I am Kökbörü’s son.
A mare was slaughtered at my feast,
And I was given the name Koyonaaly.
One who sets fire to grassy ground—
I am one of those fiery daredevils.
One who pours blood into clear water—
I am that very leopard.
Trouble has fallen on that dear head;
I am the dark eye Khan Manas looks to.
Aunt, Algara, whom you would not give when asked—
Today I shall cast a grim catching pole upon him.
That trumpet-like life of yours—
Today I shall take your head out on the plain!
You have wearied my eyes,
You have made a spectacle for my eyes.
Why have you so forgotten
Your fortunate lion Manas?”
Saying these words,
He pressed her against his saddle,
Your dear Koyonaaly!
Despairing of her precious life,
She struggled in anguish.
Then, weeping and shrieking,
She begged the boy to spare her life:
“When a foot messenger from Jelpinish
Ran past the dwelling yesterday,
‘Your daughter Külnaary
Has borne a son,’ he said.
When he came to my father Karacha
Yesterday to announce the happy news,
A thousand young mares from the herd
Were given as the messenger’s reward.
When I heard the good news,
My thoughts were shaken.
When I heard the true news of you,
My insides trembled.
Then my rib cage gave a throb;
When they said you had been born,
My heart throbbed violently.
I thought you were still not grown,
But you have grown already.
You have grown; I shall heed your words.
Nephew, spare my life—I shall go at once!”
He did not let her turn toward anything else.
He made Saykal ready;
Having half killed her,
He drove Saykal along.
When they came halfway,
Your boy spoke:
“For Manas, my father’s sworn brother,
Are you a soul that cannot burn with grief?
For Manas, my father’s sworn brother,
Are you a soul that cannot seethe with grief?
Aunt, I shall kill you,
I shall gouge out your eyes on the plain.
Otherwise, if you have hope for your life,
Go tearing your face bloody,
Go with your black hair loosened!”
Saying this, the young boy
One of the six keen steels fallen from heaven—
Zulpuqor, which Manas had obtained,
Grasped it by the hilt,
And drew it from its sheath.
When he took the sword in hand,
Saykal was filled with distress.
Her dear hair, like meadow grass,
She spread down over her breast.
Her radiant white face—
Saykal, Khan Karacha’s daughter,
Tugged and tore at it again and again.
Her bloody face torn,
Her black hair loosened:
“If sixty rivers joined,
My lord khan, you would be their rushing current.
The neck where the mountains end—
My lord khan, you are its jutting spur.
A high mountain no goose can circle,
My steadfast lord, my mighty mountain!”
Thus Khan Saykal
Entered singing her lament.
When Saykal came tearing at herself,
Manas, the dear khan,
Was coughing in deep bursts,
Lifting his head from the pillow.
He was gravely ill;
His piercing eyes barely showed,
His fine mustache lay flattened,
As though he were leaving for the world beyond.
The hero was in a terrible state!
Having entered Beijing and returned,
Having lost his champions,
Your hero was failing now.
To a corner of the whole wide world,
The boy Koyonaaly
He had sent galloping then.
“For forty days before you die,
I shall attend your rites,”
She had made this promise;
So he had the maiden Saykal tend him.
Your ruler lay in anguish,
At times able to speak,
At times unable to speak.
A grievous sickness had befallen him.
The horses on the hills, with white-marked heads,
Thoroughbreds and fleet steeds mingled—
The child to drive and tend them was young,
And all his brothers and kinsmen were enemies!
Voicing his sorrow in a groan,
Your ruler began to lament:
“After my eyes have closed,
Wide Talas will not be a people for you.
Common iron is not keen steel;
Dogs raised apart from the start are no people.
Iron pieced together will not become keen steel;
Dogs raised apart from the start will not become a people.
The six scoundrels always had treachery in their eyes;
If they had the power, those six scoundrels
Were always ready to trip me up.
Crookedness was always in their words,
Something awry was always in their eyes.
If you die when I die,
If we both die together—
Let us not settle down in the valley, my lady,
Let us not both become like a fire extinguished!
When her husband dies, a woman’s own kin become her refuge.
Scatter your gathered possessions and go;
Flee toward your own kin, Temirkhan.
When you reach Temirkhan,
Leave off your wildness, you fierce slave woman;
Braid the hair down your back.
Semetey, now six months old,
Entrust to your own brother Ysmayyl!
Have an amulet hung around his neck,
Have your brother Ysmayyl raise him.
Do not dress him in dirty clothes.
Until he reaches twelve years of age,
Do not let him know about the Kyrgyz.
Do not let him learn about his father.
The one God creates the soul;
My fierce one, my soul is departing.
Before he reaches twelve,
Entrust him to a mullah,
So he does not grow up inept.
Put a gun in his hand
And make the boy a hunter.
When he reaches twelve years of age,
Set your sights back on Talas.
If my spirit is still present,
I shall meet him upon the road.
Call Koshoy here!
Has your wish been granted?
Have Koshoy and Töshtük come?
Has what was broken been joined,
Has what was scattered been gathered,
Have you finished putting things in order?
Call the giants here,
Bring the mighty ones in here!
Let me cast my eyes upon them,
And to my friends for the world beyond
Let me offer my farewell!
Khan Koshoy of the Katagan
Was a hero favored by victory.
Eleman’s Töshtük
Was my friend from long ago.
Saykal, Karacha’s daughter,
Was a friend unto Judgment.
Kökbörü, Urumkhan’s son,
Was a friend sworn three times in one day.
My companions blessed by Kydyr, the forty heroes,
Are my companions for the world beyond.
Kanykey, who shares my esteem,
Is my precious portion of life.
The one who gave a way in a place of hardship,
Who found sight on a dark day,
Who found the right word in an unexpected crisis,
Who leaned his head against a sacred willow,
Who wrapped his feet in a thousand gold pieces,
Who, holding the banner, never stirred,
Who never shifted from his place,
Who never shrank back from an enemy,
Who never turned away at the mention of death,
Who stirred the stars in heaven with me,
Who became my friend for the world beyond,
Who joined with me when we were tiny as lice,
Who united with me when we were small as thumbs,
Who met me at the right moment,
Who was found in childhood—
My elder Bakai, the leopard,
My saint in whom I sought shelter—
Call my khan here!
Ajybai, Argynkhan’s son,
My champion rich in wisdom,
Between unbeliever and Muslim
My valiant one who went as intermediary,
Who honed his eloquent tongue,
Who spoke like a songbird before khans,
Who spoke in an unbroken flow,
Who knew no superfluous word,
Argynkhan’s son,
Who joined together what had broken,
Who, without sparing his precious life,
Before Esenkhan
